subject: Career
title: Granovetter's Strength of Weak Ties
description: A 60-second lesson on Granovetter's Strength of Weak Ties.

hook.text: 83% of people who found jobs through contacts got them through acquaintances, not close friends.

buildup.text: Mark Granovetter's 1973 paper is one of the most cited in sociology: weak ties deliver more opportunities.

discovery.text: Close friends know the same people and information you do. Acquaintances bridge to new circles.

twist.text: This means casual contacts — old colleagues, conference acquaintances — are career gold mines.

climax.text: Maintain weak ties with occasional check-ins. A yearly message keeps the bridge alive.

punchline.text: Your next opportunity lives in your weakest ties.

quiz.question: What did Granovetter's research reveal about job finding?
options: Most jobs come through acquaintances, not close friends
Close friends are the best source

details.summary: Mark Granovetter's landmark 1973 study showed that acquaintances, or weak ties, are more likely to provide novel job opportunities than close friends because they bridge different social circles and carry non-redundant information.
details.whyItMatters: Investing all networking energy in close relationships creates an echo chamber. Weak ties offer access to fresh information and opportunities your inner circle cannot see.
takeaways: Weak ties bridge separate social networks and carry unique information
Most job leads come from acquaintances rather than close friends
Maintaining a broad network of weak ties amplifies opportunity flow

faq.question: How do you maintain weak ties without it feeling transactional?
faq.answer: Low-effort touches like congratulating a connection on LinkedIn, sharing a relevant article, or sending a brief holiday greeting keep the tie alive. These gestures take seconds but keep you in someone's awareness for when opportunities arise.

faq.question: Does the strength of weak ties theory still apply in the age of social media?
faq.answer: Research confirms it does. Social media actually makes it easier to maintain weak ties at scale. LinkedIn studies show that connections two or three degrees out are the most valuable sources of job referrals, consistent with Granovetter's findings.
